metadata.title: Academic Vocabulary that Sticks
metadata.summary: A ~12-minute primer on explicit vocabulary instruction — choosing high-value words, student-friendly definitions, and multiple encounters — with an embedded example word bank, a knowledge check, and an action step.

content.body:
Vocabulary knowledge is one of the strongest correlates of reading comprehension, and it compounds: students who know more words learn more words from context. Explicit instruction cannot cover the tens of thousands of words students need — its job is to make a small set of high-value words genuinely usable, while wide reading does the volume work.

Choose words worth the time. A widely used framework (Beck, McKeown, and Kucan) sorts words into three tiers: everyday words most students already know (tier one), high-utility academic words that appear across subjects — analyze, consequence, evidence, contrast (tier two), and domain-specific technical terms — photosynthesis, denominator (tier three). Tier two words repay instruction most broadly, because they unlock text in every class.

Define in student-friendly language first. Dictionary definitions are written for people who already know the word. 'Reluctant: not wanting to do something, and maybe trying to get out of it' beats 'unwilling; disinclined.' Characterize the word — how it is used, what it goes with — rather than just labeling it.

Then engineer multiple encounters in varied contexts. A word is learned through repeated meaningful use: examples and non-examples, questions that force a decision ('Would a reluctant student volunteer first? Why not?'), quick writing and speaking uses, and morphology work — reluctant, reluctance, reluctantly — that turns one word into a family. A single introduction, however good, fades.

A glossary or word bank supports this — as a reference students return to during reading and writing, not as a list to memorize. The embedded word bank below is an example of the form: a small set of tier-two words with student-friendly definitions, ready to sit beside a text.
keyPoints: Explicit instruction covers few words; make them count and let wide reading do volume.
Prioritize tier-two words — high-utility academic words that appear across subjects.
Student-friendly definitions characterize how a word is used, not just what it labels.
Learning takes multiple meaningful encounters: examples, non-examples, decisions, morphology.
A word bank is a reference to use during reading and writing, not a memorization list.

content.instructions: This is the form in practice: six tier-two words with student-friendly definitions, the kind of word bank that sits beside a text during reading and writing.

items.def: To look at something piece by piece to figure out what it means or how it works.
Facts or details that show why something is true — what you point to when someone asks 'how do you know?'
To show how two things are different from each other.
What happens because of something else — the result, good or bad.
Not wanting to do something, and maybe trying to get out of it.
Important enough to matter and worth paying attention to.

questions.prompt: Which set is the best candidate for explicit whole-class instruction before a science text?
options: happy, run, book — words everyone knows
every unfamiliar word in the chapter
words the teacher finds personally interesting
analyze, evidence, significant — high-utility words the text leans on
questions.explanation: Tier-two academic words repay instruction across every subject; covering everything spreads the time too thin to stick.

questions.prompt: Which is the strongest STUDENT-FRIENDLY definition of 'reluctant'?
options: Not wanting to do something, and maybe trying to get out of it
questions.explanation: It characterizes how the word is used in plain language. Dictionary synonyms only help students who already know the synonyms.

questions.prompt: A teacher introduces 'consequence' well on Monday and never returns to it. The most likely outcome is:
options: Students own the word — one strong introduction is enough
The word fades; learning needs multiple meaningful encounters in varied contexts
Students learn it if it was on the word wall
questions.explanation: Vocabulary learning is incremental: examples, non-examples, forced decisions, and morphology across days do the work.

content.prompt: Look at the next text your students will read. Choose up to five tier-two words worth teaching explicitly, write a student-friendly definition for the hardest one, and name two different encounters you will engineer with it during the week.
